QF.id: AIFM CIII Fund Monitoring Reporting and Exit_48

question.text: Ms. Neha Desai, CIO of Aravalli Long-Short Fund (Cat III open-ended), observes that a mid-cap long position has gone illiquid after regulatory action on the issuer. Single-investee exposure is now 11% of NAV (above the 10% open-ended limit). The best immediate action is to:

answer.text: Hide the exposure until NAV recovery
Side-pocket the illiquid position and freeze main-scheme subscriptions pending NAV recompute
Increase leverage to buy more of the affected name

explanation.text: The Logic: The best immediate response to a single illiquid stressed long that has pushed concentration above the open-ended limit is to segregate the affected position into a side-pocket and freeze main-scheme subscriptions while NAV is recomputed. This isolates the illiquidity event from the rest of the portfolio, preserves fairness between existing investors and any new subscribers, and brings the main scheme back into compliance with the concentration limit on a forward-looking basis. Hiding the exposure or increasing leverage worsens the breach and the fiduciary problem; winding-up is disproportionate to a single-position illiquidity event. The Trap: A is a breach of disclosure and risk-management obligations. C compounds the concentration breach and burns leverage capacity on the very name that caused the problem. D triggers fund-level winding-up, which is far out of proportion to a single illiquid long position. Note: The cited NISM Series XIX-E workbook pages (77, 317, 408) support Cat III concentration limits, illiquid-security valuation, and suspension of redemptions/new subscriptions in exceptional circumstances, but do not describe side-pocket creation or specific side-pocket fee/subscription mechanics. The framing above is general industry/fund-management practice rather than a workbook-page citation.
